intro: The last two units followed the Qur'an's story: Mecca, Medina, the man Muslims call the Prophet, and the moments tradition says each verse answered. This unit turns from the story to the ideas. What does the book say about God? About the sky, the sea and the camel? About angels, prophets and earlier scriptures? About the day Muslims believe every deed will be weighed? And what does it ask of the people who read it: how to treat parents, orphans, neighbors, strangers and enemies?

You will read passages close up in Pickthall's 1930 translation, with older translations beside it for comparison, and with commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explaining what they saw. You will meet Muslims who read the same lines differently: classical jurists and modern scholars, Sunni and Shia, Sufi poets and philosophers. The course never tells you which reading is right. It shows you what the text says and how its readers have used it.

By the end you will be able to explain tawhid and the names of God, describe what the Qur'an says about creation and the Last Day, name the prophets and books it shares with the Bible, and read a verse about war, food, family or charity with the verses around it and its occasion. That last skill matters most. A verse alone in a box proves anything; a verse on its page teaches something.
bigQuestion: What does the Qur'an teach about God and about how to live, and why does the context of a verse change what its readers take from it?

timeline.t: Muslim tradition says the first verses come to Muhammad in Mecca: "Read!" (96:1–5).
Meccan surahs stress one God, the signs in nature, and the Last Day; the poor and the orphan are defended.
The hijra to Medina; the surahs that follow add law on family, charity, food and fighting.
The battle of Badr; commentators place the verses on fighting, such as 2:190–193, around this time.
The battle of Uhud leaves widows and orphans; tradition links rules in Surah 4 to this period.
Muhammad enters Mecca and pardons most of the city, citing Yusuf's words in 12:92 according to tradition.
Muhammad dies in Medina; the Qur'an's text is gathered into one book in the following decades.
The founders of the major law schools, Sunni and Shia, teach and die; fiqh takes shape.
Al-Bukhari dies; his hadith collection becomes the most trusted among Sunni Muslims.
Al-Tabari dies, leaving a vast commentary that records early readings of each verse.
Al-Ghazali dies; his writing shapes how mercy, the names of God and the purposes of law are read.
Marmaduke Pickthall publishes his English translation, the text this course quotes.

test.q: Surah 112, Al-Ikhlas, says of God that:
choices: He rested on the seventh day
He begets not and was not begotten
test.why: Al-Ikhlas states tawhid: God is one, begets not, was not begotten, and has no equal.

test.q: The two names in the basmala, ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim, both come from a root meaning:
test.why: Both names come from the root for mercy, which Ibn Kathir explains as mercy in God's nature and mercy in action.

choices: A description of God's power and knowledge that many Muslims recite for protection
test.why: Ayat al-Kursi lists God's attributes, from never sleeping to holding the heavens and earth, and is recited after prayer and before sleep.

test.q: Qur'an 88:17–20 asks its hearers to look at the camel, the sky, the hills and the earth in order to:
choices: See them as signs pointing to one Creator
test.why: The Qur'an calls things in nature ayat, signs, and these four questions ask hearers to see evidence of a maker.

test.q: What does the Qur'an say happened after the six days of creation, in contrast with Genesis 2:2?
test.why: Qur'an 50:38 says no weariness touched God, which Muslim commentators contrast with the word "rested" in Genesis.

test.q: In the Qur'an, angels and jinn differ in that:
choices: Angels are made of fire and jinn of light
Jinn can choose belief or unbelief, while angels do not disobey
Angels appear only in Medinan surahs
test.why: Surah 72 shows jinn on different paths, and 66:6 says angels do not disobey God.

test.q: The Qur'an names Musa (Moses) more than any other prophet. What do Muslim scholars say about why Muhammad is named so rarely?
choices: The book is addressed to him, so it need not name him
He was not considered a prophet until 632
Arabic had no word for his name
test.why: Since the Qur'an speaks to Muhammad, scholars explain, it tells earlier prophets' stories as lessons for him rather than naming him.

test.q: Which book does the Qur'an say was given to Isa (Jesus)?
test.why: The Injil, the Gospel, is the book the Qur'an connects with Isa; the Tawrat goes with Musa and the Zabur with Dawud.

test.q: Qur'an 99:7–8 says that on the Last Day a person will see:
choices: Even an atom's weight of good or evil they did
Nothing until the scales are hidden
test.why: Surah 99 names the smallest weight its hearers could picture to say that judgment leaves nothing out.

test.q: Qur'an 17:23 joins two commands in one sentence. They are:
choices: Worship none but God, and be kind to parents
Pray five times and face Mecca
Give the mahr and free the captive
test.why: 17:23 puts worship of God alone and kindness to parents side by side, and forbids even saying "uff" to them.

test.q: Which is the correct pairing of a verse and its subject?
test.why: 9:60 lists the eight kinds of receivers of zakat; 2:173 is on food, 5:32 on the value of one life, 4:135 on justice.
2:190 permits fighting those who fight you and says not to begin hostilities, for God does not love aggressors.

test.q: How do commentators read 9:5 in light of 9:4?
choices: As cancelling the rules on food
As aimed at tribes that broke their treaties, since 9:4 exempts those who kept them
As a verse about the Byzantines
test.why: 9:4 exempts treaty-keepers, so Ibn Kathir and others read 9:5 as directed at treaty-breakers in a specific war.

test.q: Which statement about "no compulsion in religion" (2:256) is accurate?
choices: Most classical scholars held it was cancelled
Al-Tabari links it to parents in Medina forbidden to force their children's faith
test.why: Al-Tabari reports the occasion as parents wishing to force children raised among the Jewish tribes; most scholars did not accept its cancellation.

test.q: Which of these belongs to fiqh rather than to the Qur'an's own words?
choices: The zakat rate of two and a half percent
test.why: The Qur'an names zakat's receivers but not its rate; the rate comes from hadith and the jurists, the fiqh layer.

write.prompt: Does reading a verse with the verses around it change its meaning? Choose 2:190–193 or 5:32–33 or 2:255–256. Quote or paraphrase the verses (surah:ayah, Pickthall 1930), describe their occasion as al-Tabari or Ibn Kathir report it, and explain two different ways Muslim readers have read them.
tips: Cite each verse as surah:ayah and name the surah and the translation.
Say "Muslims believe" or "al-Tabari reports"; never say what is true, only what the text says and how readers read it.
Give at least two Muslim readings and show what each reader does with the verses the other stresses.
Use the unit's terms: asbab al-nuzul, naskh, fitnah, fiqh.
Compare readings; do not rank them or judge the tradition.
